title: Who Are the People of Palestine?
subtitle: A respectful discussion about the people of Palestine, with focus on historical context and the relevance of the Palestinian cause to Islam.
summary: Palestinians are a diverse people whose identity grew from local communities, family networks, Arabic language and culture, religious life, displacement, and political organization. Understanding that history helps readers discuss Palestine with accuracy and human dignity.

sections.title: Who Are the People of Palestine?
sections.body: Palestinians include Muslims, Christians, and people of other or no religious commitments. Families live in towns and villages across historic Palestine and in a global diaspora. Their identity is shaped by language, local memory, family life, worship, work, and attachment to particular places. It describes a people and a national identity; it does not mean that every Palestinian shares the same politics or personal beliefs.

sections.title: Identity Is Historical and Personal
sections.body:
Modern national identities develop through family networks, institutions, education, language, religious communities, migration, and political change. Palestine was a geographic name long before modern nationalism, while a specifically Palestinian national consciousness developed gradually. In the late Ottoman period, towns, newspapers, schools, trade networks, municipal bodies, and religious institutions connected local communities. Under the British Mandate, political associations, elections, the press, and opposition to competing national projects made Palestinian national politics more explicit.

Rashid Khalidi's Palestinian Identity emphasizes overlapping local, Arab, Syrian, Ottoman, and Palestinian loyalties. Beshara Doumani's Rediscovering Palestine shows how families, merchants, farmers, and local institutions shaped public life in Ottoman Palestine. James L. Gelvin places these developments within the wider history of the conflict. These historians differ in emphasis, but together they show that Palestinian identity was historically formed rather than suddenly invented in 1948.

Local, Arab, religious, and Palestinian identities could overlap. This history does not erase Jewish, Christian, Muslim, Samaritan, Armenian, Bedouin, or other connections to the land, and it does not make Palestinians a single political bloc. It does, however, explain why Palestinians understand themselves as a people with a real history and continuing attachment to their homeland.

sections.title: Key Events in Modern Palestinian History
sections.body:
Several events frame the modern Palestinian experience. The 1917 Balfour Declaration and the British Mandate placed competing national projects within one territory. The 1947 United Nations partition recommendation and the 1948 war were followed by the Nakba (catastrophe), when more than 700,000 Palestinians were displaced from their homes and became refugees. Historians continue to debate particular causes and episodes, but the scale of displacement and its lasting effect are not in doubt.

The Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) was established in 1964 as an umbrella organization for Palestinian political factions. After the 1967 war, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza came under Israeli military occupation, reshaping Palestinian political and social life.

The First Intifada began in 1987 as a mass uprising involving strikes, demonstrations, civil disobedience, and armed violence. It helped bring the Palestinian question back to the center of diplomacy and was followed by the 1993 Oslo process, in which Israel and the PLO recognized one another. The Second Intifada began in 2000 after the collapse of the peace process and escalating confrontations, bringing grave suffering to Palestinian and Israeli civilians. These milestones do not explain every later development, but they help readers understand displacement, political organization, and the continuing Palestinian attachment to home.

sections.title: Start With Human Dignity
sections.body: When reading about Palestine, begin with the basic fact that the people being discussed are human beings with names, families, grief, hopes, and ordinary responsibilities. Distinguish a government, an armed group, a religious tradition, and a civilian population. Dates, authorship, and context matter, especially when a claim is used to judge an entire people. Islamic ethics requires truthfulness and justice: the Quran commands believers to stand firm for justice, even when it is difficult (Quran 4:135), and teaches that peoples and tribes were made to know one another rather than claim racial superiority (Quran 49:13).

sections.title: Key Takeaways: Who Are the People of Palestine?
sections.body: Palestinians are a diverse people with layered local, religious, cultural, and national identities. Their modern identity developed through life in Ottoman and Mandate-era Palestine, displacement in 1948, occupation after 1967, political organization, and enduring attachment to home. Learning this history does not require hostility toward another community; it requires honesty, compassion, and justice.

quranVerses.arabic: ۞ يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ كُونُوا۟ قَوَّٰمِينَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ شُهَدَآءَ لِلَّهِ وَلَوْ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِكُمْ أَوِ ٱلْوَٰلِدَيْنِ وَٱلْأَقْرَبِينَ ۚ إِن يَكُنْ غَنِيًّا أَوْ فَقِيرًۭا فَٱللَّهُ أَوْلَىٰ بِهِمَا ۖ فَلَا تَتَّبِعُوا۟ ٱلْهَوَىٰٓ أَن تَعْدِلُوا۟ ۚ وَإِن تَلْوُۥٓا۟ أَوْ تُعْرِضُوا۟ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ خَبِيرًۭا
quranVerses.translation: O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives. Whether one is rich or poor, Allah is more worthy of both. So follow not [personal] inclination, lest you not be just. And if you distort [your testimony] or refuse [to give it], then indeed Allah is ever, with what you do, Acquainted.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ إِنَّا خَلَقْنَٰكُم مِّن ذَكَرٍۢ وَأُنثَىٰ وَجَعَلْنَٰكُمْ شُعُوبًۭا وَقَبَآئِلَ لِتَعَارَفُوٓا۟ ۚ إِنَّ أَكْرَمَكُمْ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ أَتْقَىٰكُمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ خَبِيرٌۭ
quranVerses.translation: O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Acquainted.

furtherReading.title: Palestinian Identity: The Construction of Modern National Consciousness
furtherReading.author: Rashid Khalidi
furtherReading.note: A major scholarly study of the development of Palestinian national consciousness; read alongside other historians for differing emphases.

furtherReading.title: The Palestinians: From Peasants to Revolutionaries
furtherReading.author: Rosemary Sayigh
furtherReading.note: An influential social history that foregrounds Palestinian voices and displacement; its perspective should be read alongside other histories.

furtherReading.title: Rediscovering Palestine: Merchants and Peasants in Jabal Nablus, 1700-1900
furtherReading.author: Beshara B. Doumani
furtherReading.note: A social and economic history of Ottoman Palestine that grounds national-identity discussions in local institutions, families, and regional life.

furtherReading.title: The Israel-Palestine Conflict: A History
furtherReading.author: James L. Gelvin
furtherReading.note: An accessible survey that places Palestinian identity, the Mandate, 1948, 1967, the PLO, and the Intifadas within the wider conflict.

furtherReading.title: Armed Struggle and the Search for State: The Palestinian National Movement, 1949-1993
furtherReading.author: Yezid Sayigh
furtherReading.note: A detailed history of Palestinian political organization, including the PLO and the movement's changing strategies.
